title: Hokusai
passages: Katsushika Hokusai was born in the autumn of 1760 in Edo, the busy city that is now called Tokyo, Japan. In Edo, crowds gathered to buy colorful printed pictures of actors, travelers and famous places, and some cost about as much as a simple bowl of noodles. As a boy of about 14, Hokusai became an APPRENTICE to a carver, learning to cut pictures into blocks of wood. At 18 he joined the studio of the artist Katsukawa Shunsho. He was famously RESTLESS: he changed his art name more than 30 times and is said to have moved house about 93 times.

Hokusai's most famous work came when he was past 70. From about 1830 to 1832, he published a series of WOODBLOCK prints called Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. The best loved one, The Great Wave off Kanagawa, shows a giant curling wave about to crash over three fishing boats, with tiny Mount Fuji far in the distance. He used a bright blue called PRUSSIAN blue, which had come to Japan from faraway Europe. Hokusai kept drawing until he died on 10 May 1849, at about 88 years old. Near the end, he said that with five more years he could become a true artist. Later, painters in France studied his waves with wonder.
